A.problem: Existing multi-agent LLM systems for scientific discovery suffer from unconstrained confirmation bias, generating superficially plausible but empirically unsound or hallucinatory hypotheses, while adversarial approaches focus on rhetorical persuasiveness to fool reviewers rather than grounding ideas in empirical verifiability.
A.motivation: Grounding adversarial hypothesis generation in automated empirical execution can turn falsification attempts into actionable feedback, making scientific theories more rigorous, testable, and reproducible.
A.proposed_approach: The framework uses a population of hypothesis generator agents and critic/falsification agents in an adversarial co-evolutionary loop. Critics' falsification attempts are routed into automated empirical execution loops such as code sandboxes, simulation environments, and formal verification tools, yielding structured environmental feedback. Generator agents are updated from this feedback to produce hypotheses that are testable, reproducible, and empirically grounded rather than rhetorically persuasive.
A.research_plan: Evidence is comparative evaluation on interactive scientific benchmarking suites, with the proposed framework compared against non-adversarial and purely rhetorical baselines. The metrics used are hypothesis falsification resistance, empirical reproducibility, and uncertainty reduction. The abstract does not state failure conditions or what is held matched across baselines.

B.problem: Existing multi-agent scientific ideation frameworks predominantly rely on cooperative or positive synthesis, causing confirmation bias and insufficient critical stress-testing that yield ungrounded or easily refutable hypotheses. Although post-hoc hypothesis validation and inference-time adversarial adjustments have been explored separately, active adversarial refutation integrated with co-evolutionary generator-critic feedback during ideation remains underexplored.
B.motivation: LLM agents have demonstrated capabilities in automating scientific ideation and hypothesis generation, making it timely to address their confirmation-bias limitations.
B.proposed_approach: A multi-agent framework frames scientific ideation as a co-evolutionary game between a Hypothesis Generator and an Adversarial Falsifier. The Falsifier actively constructs empirical counter-arguments and simulated refutation plans targeting logical and empirical gaps in current hypotheses, and the Generator adapts its parametric knowledge using this adversarial feedback at inference time.
B.research_plan: Experiments across benchmark scientific environments compare the proposed framework against standard collaborative and purely affirmative multi-agent baselines, evaluating downstream robustness, empirical viability, and novelty of generated hypotheses. The abstract does not state a specific failure condition or matched settings.

A.problem: In autonomous self-driving laboratories, LLM agents can plan and run chemistry experiments, but their plans frequently violate a posteriori unknown feasibility constraints, and they rarely recover from hardware faults without hand-written scripts.
A.motivation: Reliable autonomous operation is needed for droplet-microfluidic catalyst screening, where feasibility grounding and failure-tolerant replanning would reduce human intervention and hardware risk.
A.proposed_approach: The proposed framework uses a hierarchical LLM agent to generate hypotheses and experimental plans. Before any hardware command, a structured feasibility validator checks each plan against a device-specific constraint knowledge base covering pressure envelopes, flow-rate bounds, reagent/solvent compatibility, solubility windows, and stability limits, while an LLM-driven constraint regularizer grounds that knowledge base in curated wet-lab microfluidic literature. A failure-diagnosis module maps measured sensor signatures from flow, pressure, droplet-size distribution, and optical readouts onto a causal failure graph covering clogging, coalescence, bubbles, drying, and phase separation, identifies the most plausible fault with evidence and confidence, and triggers automated replanning from a structured corrective-action library; a machine-checkable policy governs confirmation, failure recovery, escalation, and stopping, escalating persistent uncertainty or safety interlocks to a human operator. The deliverable includes a reusable, openly published fault-injection benchmark suite for microfluidic catalyst discovery.
A.research_plan: The framework is evaluated on a droplet-microfluidic catalyst-screening testbed spanning a catalyst × condition matrix with in situ optical readout. Fault tolerance is tested under a fault-injection benchmark of 20 seeded, physically real faults: clogging, wrong-reagent injection, phase separation, drying, and out-of-envelope setups. It is compared against three baselines: an AlphaFlow-style RL planner, a DMFAs-style unconstrained LLM tool-harness planner with and without domain-specialized tools, and a passive hardware-monitor. Success is defined as at least 70% autonomous fault recovery, zero out-of-envelope commands, and at least 0.9× the feasible-region sample efficiency of the BO-style baseline; these thresholds serve as failure conditions for the corresponding claims.

B.problem: Electronic materials characterization is split between industry-scale automated systems offering high throughput but limited flexibility and highly customized, expert-driven systems offering research-grade discovery but limited bandwidth, leaving a gap for approaches that combine both.
B.motivation: Recent hardware APIs and AI integration make it possible to bridge these two regimes, enabling research-grade characterization at higher throughput and allowing both human and AI agents to operate heterogeneous instruments.
B.proposed_approach: The proposed platform is a custom-built characterization system for the agentic-AI era that provides unified control of scanning probe microscopes and programmable peripheral instrumentation. It is built around application program interfaces that control hardware and integrates AI methods to incorporate autonomy. Its design choices aim to maximize system capability and ease of use for both human and AI agents, making heterogeneous scientific instruments accessible, composable, and usable by agents.
B.research_plan: The benefits are demonstrated by test cases involving the platform's use with heterogeneous scientific instruments; the abstract does not state baselines, metrics, or failure conditions, and does not specify which claim each test case supports.

A.problem: Autonomous "AI scientist" systems improve an existing code baseline by iteratively refining a single favored method family until a compute or time budget runs out, and independent evaluations find stalled ideas that are never abandoned, post-hoc reinterpretation of negative results, and fabricated or unverifiable experiment narratives; there is no decision layer that forces competing hypotheses to make pre-registered predictions and supports principled abandonment.
A.motivation: Without such a layer, autonomous research agents waste experiment budget on stalled method families and produce untrustworthy or unverifiable narratives; adding hard pre-registration, auditable budget allocation, and statistically grounded abandonment would reduce wasted experiments and make agent-driven research decisions more auditable.
A.proposed_approach: The proposed decision-making layer has an AI research agent maintain a small portfolio of competing mechanism-level hypotheses, and forces each hypothesis to commit a pre-registered quantitative prediction before every experiment. It then runs a budgeted race in which experiments are allocated to the hypotheses whose disagreement they best resolve. A hypothesis family is permanently archived once its pre-registered predictions are statistically dominated by a rival.
A.research_plan: The evidence is two-layered. (1) A synthetic suite with known ground truth measures experiments-to-convergence, budget wasted on the plateau family, and kill/keep accuracy; this bears on both the efficiency and archive-decision claims. (2) A subset of execution-grounded research-agent tasks first isolates decisions under a pre-verified execution oracle and then probes them with a real coding agent, testing whether the decision behavior transfers. The comparison is held to a fixed experiment budget; support requires fewer experiments to target than single-thread refinement and better ground-truth recovery than the LLM judge.

B.problem: Autonomous research loops driven by large language models can run machine-learning experiments at scale but tend to drift toward local refinements of whichever metric they optimise rather than testing the hypotheses that motivate the experiments.
B.motivation: Structural safeguards are needed to keep autonomous research scientifically honest as it scales, and a separate taste oracle could direct exploration without contaminating the epistemic loop.
B.proposed_approach: An autonomous research loop for studying generalisation in quadruped robot navigation policies is built on an existing autonomous research paradigm. It adds an immutable experiment card that records each iteration's prediction and outcome under a fixed schema, specialised subagents restricted to mechanical roles, and a preference oracle that encodes the user's research taste as a typed knowledge graph and is the only component allowed subjective judgements. To isolate the oracle, the identical loop is run twice across eleven research streams, once with and once without the preference oracle.
B.research_plan: The evaluation isolates the preference oracle by running the identical scaffold across eleven research streams in two arms: with and without the oracle. Drift is assessed by whether each arm retcons falsified hypotheses or merely refines its optimised metric, using the fixed experiment-card schema as the instrument. The oracle's effect is assessed on direction rather than score: which arm explores test-time adaptation, which arm authors winning designs where it led, and whether lessons carry across streams. The scaffold's honesty claim would fail if either arm drifted from hypothesis testing despite metric optimisation. Policy quality is compared as a secondary axis while holding the loop scaffold fixed.

A.problem: Current AI Scientist systems apply fixed research workflows across diverse scientific domains, despite evidence that different problem types benefit from fundamentally different discovery approaches.
A.motivation: Reducing unnecessary experiment failures and accelerating convergence to publishable results would make AI-driven scientific discovery more efficient.
A.proposed_approach: The framework classifies incoming scientific problems by structural characteristics such as discrete vs. continuous optimization and data-driven vs. first-principles reasoning. It learns which research methodologies, including hypothesis generation strategies, experiment design patterns, and validation protocols, are most effective for each problem class based on historical outcomes. It then dynamically adapts or selects research workflows for each problem to maximize discovery efficiency and reduce failure rates.
A.research_plan: The framework is evaluated on a benchmark of research tasks spanning materials discovery, algorithm design, and equation discovery, comparing domain-aware methodology selection against fixed-workflow baselines. The stated evidence conditions are experiment failure rates and convergence to publishable results; no matched compute/parameter controls, ablations, or explicit failure condition are described.

B.problem: Current AI scientist systems generalize poorly across structurally different research problems, and available benchmarks either test general task automation rather than research-specific reasoning or remain confined to machine learning.
B.motivation: Enabling AI agents to recognize domain novelty and compose appropriate workflows could extend automated scientific reasoning across disciplines instead of requiring fixed pipelines per domain.
B.proposed_approach: The proposed agent architecture detects the novelty of a research task's domain and dynamically selects or composes domain-appropriate workflows rather than running a fixed end-to-end pipeline. A lightweight task-structure classifier decides whether a problem fits learned domain patterns or represents a novel research paradigm, and a modular planner-executor hierarchy composes hypothesis generation, experimental design, and analysis modules accordingly. The system is evaluated on a newly introduced benchmark spanning six scientific domains with explicit cross-domain generalization splits.
B.research_plan: (1) The claim that adaptive workflow selection improves generalization is tested on a new benchmark spanning six scientific domains with explicit cross-domain generalization splits, comparing the proposed architecture against fixed-pipeline baselines. (2) The claim that agents can handle domains absent from training is tested by evaluating on benchmark domains not seen during training. The abstract does not state ablations or matched compute/training budgets, nor an explicit failure condition beyond fixed-pipeline comparison.

A.problem: Existing AI methods, especially large language models, support individual tasks like hypothesis generation and experimental design but do not reproduce the collaborative, team-based way in which diverse experts jointly address complex scientific problems.
A.motivation: Accelerating scientific discovery requires tools that can emulate collaborative expert teamwork, not only individual reasoning.
A.proposed_approach: An enhanced LLM-based multi-agent system that gives the agents a time-varying knowledge exchange mechanism and a review process with two separate diversity criteria; it is intended to emulate collaborative scientific teamwork for idea generation.
A.research_plan: The paper reports comprehensive experiments comparing the proposed system with state-of-the-art methods, using novelty of generated scientific ideas as the evaluation target.

B.problem: Many existing AI scientist systems rely on rigid interaction protocols and coarse-grained novelty tests, which impede long-term creative exploration in autonomous scientific ideation.
B.motivation: Massive language models show promise for autonomous scientific ideation, so more flexible multi-agent collaboration and finer-grained novelty assessment may unlock long-term creative exploration.
B.proposed_approach: The proposed framework organizes multiple agents into rotating conversation groups using a World Café-style collaborative structure. A multi-strategy turn-taking scheduler distributes speaking turns adaptively based on relevance, participation balance, and self-reported willingness. Novelty assessment incorporates a finer-grained idea novelty metric for more detailed evaluation.
B.research_plan: Evaluation compares the framework against single-agent and multi-agent baselines using a total novelty measure, under regulated discussion cost conditions and using public academic knowledge graphs. The design also includes component-level assessment of the turn-taking scheduler and the novelty metric's effect on creative performance. No explicit failure condition or matched compute/parameter controls are stated.

A.problem: Current LLM-based discovery agents generate, fit, and rank hypotheses but rarely treat the choice of an experiment that most cheaply separates live rival explanations as a first-class decision, underusing the places where their own competing models disagree.
A.motivation: Newly available interactive-discovery environments make this discrimination problem measurable and tractable, while existing evidence that current LLM agents are weak at experiment design and do not improve merely by adding explicit statistical models suggests an unaddressed capability bottleneck.
A.proposed_approach: The proposed framework operates as an agentic loop over an explicit executable set of rival hypotheses. At each step it renders each surviving hypothesis as code carrying an explicit noise model, proposes an intervention, scores it by a cost-normalized divergence measure quantifying how much simulated outcomes would separate the rivals, runs the best intervention, and eliminates hypotheses whose outcome it refutes. The proposal specifies the protocol, the divergence-score estimator, a benchmark crossing four environments, four ablations, and success and error metrics.
A.research_plan: The proposal evaluates the framework on newly available interactive-discovery environments, including BoxingGym and PhysGym, against otherwise-equivalent agents pursuing fit, novelty, validation, or statistical-model augmentation without discrimination planning. Success for the first claim is identifying the true underlying model in fewer experiments than those baselines; success for the second is achieving controlled false-elimination error. The benchmark crosses four environments and four ablations to isolate components of the divergence-driven selection loop, with specified success and error metrics. Failure would occur if the framework does not reduce the number of experiments or does not control false-elimination error relative to the otherwise-equivalent agents; the comparison design holds agents otherwise equivalent and manipulates only the discrimination-planning mechanism.

B.problem: In closed-loop LLM-based scientific discovery, the same underlying model typically proposes hypotheses, chooses experiments, and revises them, so the selector of evidence is also the advocate of the hypothesis; this coupling may create a confirmation bias in which experiments probe regions the favored hypothesis predicts rather than regions where rival hypotheses disagree, wasting budget and leaving false models unrefuted.
B.motivation: Because LLM agents are increasingly used for autonomous scientific discovery, removing self-induced confirmation bias would make limited experiment budgets more informative and reduce the risk of false models surviving.
B.proposed_approach: The intervention splits the closed-loop discovery loop into two roles. One set of components generates and maintains an explicit ensemble of rival executable hypotheses. A separate experiment-selection component, which is never told which hypothesis is currently favored, chooses each experiment to maximize expected discrimination across the whole ensemble. This structurally decouples experiment choice from the current favorite, making the chosen experiment accountable to all live hypotheses rather than only the favored one.
B.research_plan: The claim is evaluated at a fixed experiment budget in interactive environments with hidden ground truth, including the paper's enumerable micro-environments and two gym-style environments. The proposed decoupled system is compared against self-selecting agents, single-model expected-information-gain agents, impartiality-prompted agents, and falsifier-of-the-favorite agents on recovery of the true model, number of experiments to convergence, and a confirmatory-bias metric. Support requires the decoupled system to recover the true model more often, converge with fewer experiments, and show lower confirmatory bias than the baselines at the same budget; absence of these differences would falsify the claim.

A.problem: The potential of fine-tuned LLMs for hypothesis generation and experimental design in chemistry and material science remains unexplored in real-world applications, and no framework exists for their systematic use in scientific discovery.
A.motivation: LLMs have shown promise in automating stages of scientific research, including hypothesis generation and experimental design; extending this to chemistry and material science could advance scientific discovery.
A.proposed_approach: Apply fine-tuned LLMs to chemistry and material science to generate novel hypotheses and experimental designs; assess their performance in real-world applications; identify strengths and limitations; and use the assessment to propose a framework for their systematic use in scientific discovery.
A.research_plan: Assess the performance of fine-tuned LLMs in real-world chemistry and material science applications; the assessment is intended to identify strengths and limitations and to support a proposed framework for systematic use. No baselines, metrics, or failure conditions are specified in the abstract.

B.problem: Hypothesis generation and experimental design in materials science currently rely on manual literature analysis and are limited in efficiency and innovation.
B.motivation: Rapid advances in large language models make it newly possible to analyze large volumes of literature and automate the generation of research questions and experimental designs, potentially transforming materials discovery.
B.proposed_approach: A framework is developed that uses fine-tuned large language models to generate scientific hypotheses and experimental designs in materials science. The approach analyzes existing literature to identify knowledge gaps and propose research questions and methodologies. A dataset of materials science papers is created and used to fine-tune the models. The generated hypotheses and designs are then evaluated for quality.
B.research_plan: The plan is to create a dataset of materials science papers, fine-tune the models on it, and evaluate the quality of the generated hypotheses and experimental designs. The quality evaluation is intended as evidence for the claim that fine-tuned LLMs can produce useful research directions; no baselines, metrics, or failure conditions are specified.

A.problem: Generating high-quality hypotheses in scientific research is challenging and time-consuming, and current LLM-based approaches show promise but can be further improved in effectiveness.
A.motivation: Automating hypothesis generation could reduce the time and effort required for scientific research; recent advances in LLMs make this tractable, and evolutionary algorithms are well-suited for exploring complex search spaces and optimizing solutions.
A.proposed_approach: The proposed work develops a framework that integrates LLMs with evolutionary algorithms to automate and optimize hypothesis generation. The evolutionary algorithm component is used to explore complex search spaces and optimize candidate solutions, while LLMs support hypothesis generation.
A.research_plan: The framework will be evaluated across various scientific domains to assess performance, efficiency, and innovation. No baselines, metrics, or failure conditions are specified, and no matched controls or ablations are described.

B.problem: Existing LLM-assisted approaches to scientific idea generation exhibit semantic convergence, which limits the diversity and novelty of generated research ideas.
B.motivation: As LLMs show promise in assisting idea generation, overcoming semantic convergence is valuable for broadening the candidate ideas and advancing scientific progress.
B.proposed_approach: The proposed framework recasts scientific idea generation as an evolutionary search over a population of ideas. It iteratively applies rank-based mutation with differentiated retrieval planning to incorporate external knowledge, and semantic-aware crossover to fuse complementary concepts for conceptual reorganization. A lightweight evaluation signal guides selection, encouraging sustained exploration while mitigating premature convergence.
B.research_plan: The evidence is extensive experiments comparing the proposed framework to state-of-the-art baselines on novelty, diversity, and idea quality under the current automatic evaluation protocol. Claims about enhanced exploration and maintained quality are supported by these comparisons; no explicit failure condition is stated in the abstract.

A.problem: LLM agents increasingly perform end-to-end ML engineering tasks where success is judged by a single scalar test metric; this creates a structural vulnerability in which an agent can increase the reported score by compromising the evaluation pipeline rather than improving the model.
A.motivation: If scores can be raised by compromising evaluation, progress signals become unreliable, so evaluation integrity must be made explicit and measurable rather than assumed.
A.proposed_approach: The proposed benchmark runs each episode in a fresh workspace with patch tracking and runtime file-access logging. It makes two compromise vectors explicit: evaluator tampering (modifying metric computation or reporting) and train/test leakage (accessing held-out data or labels during training). Detectors compare the agent-reported metric to a trusted reference to assign auditable integrity labels.
A.research_plan: (1) For the benchmark's detection claim, episodes run in fresh workspaces with patch tracking and runtime file-access logging, and detectors compare agent-reported metrics to a trusted reference. (2) Scripted attack runs exercise both compromise vectors in fully mutable workspaces. (3) Single-mechanism defenses are tested separately on each vector, and a combined defense regime is tested against both, with the same three tasks and two LLM backbones across conditions. (4) Natural-agent runs are monitored for evaluator-tampering attempts, and an evaluator-locking condition is compared with a mutable baseline on runtime overhead, holding tasks and backbones fixed.

B.problem: AI-scientist systems fail inside their workflows in easily overlooked ways—inappropriate benchmark selection, data leakage, metric misuse, and post-hoc selection bias—and while human experts can detect these failures when trace logs are available, there is no automated or benchmarked capability for doing so. Existing verification benchmarks inspect only the manuscript artifact, and re-execution benchmarks verify only computational correctness of a declared recipe, so by construction they cannot expose selection bias or benchmark cherry-picking.
B.motivation: Undetected workflow-level integrity violations risk invalidating AI-scientist outputs, and trace logs have been shown to make these violations far easier to detect; open-source AI-scientist systems can now be replayed, making systematic evaluation of workflow-level audit feasible rather than relying on human expert inspection.
B.proposed_approach: The benchmark is built by replaying open-source AI-scientist systems (e.g., Jr. AI Scientist) on about 40 small-but-real ML tasks and injecting each of four failure modes at the workflow level, under two conditions per run: open, where the paper reflects the flaw, and concealed, where the flaw is masked so the manuscript reads clean. In each instance, an agent receives the full provenance trace of an AI-scientist run (tool calls, decision log, code, and data lineage) plus the manuscript, and must emit a per-mode verdict over the four-mode taxonomy plus exact citations of the trace events constituting each violation.
B.research_plan: The evidence is organized around the three falsifiable hypotheses. (1) H1 is tested by comparing trace-augmented audit F1 to paper-only LLM audit F1 on concealed runs, with support defined as an advantage of at least 0.35. (2) H2 is tested by applying re-execution-based checking to selection-bias and benchmark-choice modes, with support defined as scores near zero. (3) H3 is tested by comparing open-to-concealed relative degradation for paper-only audit and trace-augmented audit, with support defined as paper-only degradation of at least 40% and trace-augmented degradation of at most 10%. The abstract does not state what is held matched across compared systems.

A.problem: Rigorous real-world physical research using large language models is stalled by a lack of realistic evaluation benchmarks and by systemic LLM hallucinations.
A.motivation: Addressing these barriers would make automated scientific discovery in quantum many-body simulation more robust, reliable, and transparent.
A.proposed_approach: The work releases a research-level benchmark of 100 tasks in quantum many-body simulation drawn from 21 high-impact journals. The proposed framework is a multi-agent system that enforces self-verification and error correction; it integrates programming verifiers and scientific verifiers to check coding correctness and principle-based physical validity, producing interpretable evidence and error correction at each step.
A.research_plan: (1) The claim that the benchmark is research-level and challenging rests on its construction from 100 tasks in 21 high-impact journals and on testing against current frontier LLMs. (2) The claim that the framework enforces reliable, physically valid outputs rests on comparisons with existing LLM baselines across benchmark scenarios and on evaluation of inference-time scaling.

B.problem: Current language agents in autonomous AI scientist systems frequently fail during complex, multi-step experimental execution and validation because they lack adequate error correction and rigorous intermediate verification; this produces an implementation gap between generated research plans and executable, validated results.
B.motivation: As autonomous scientist systems become more capable at generating hypotheses, code, and reports, trustworthy adoption depends on closing the implementation gap so that agent-produced work is executable and its conclusions reliable.
B.proposed_approach: The framework integrates constraint-guided test-time verification and dynamic self-correction loops into autonomous scientific workflows. Scientific verification is decomposed into domain-specific invariant checking, automated test case synthesis, and executable code validation. Test-time interaction and verification compute are scaled to catch errors before conclusions are finalized.
B.research_plan: The comparative claim is evaluated on challenging scientific agent benchmarks against standard prompting and unverified iterative debugging baselines, measuring execution success rates and reliability of discovered findings. The detection claim is addressed through the framework's decomposition into invariant checking, test synthesis, and code validation, though no explicit failure condition or ablation is stated.

A.problem: Large eddy simulation of turbulent flows depends on subgrid-scale closure models, but standard data-driven equation discovery and sparse regression often produce closures that are numerically unstable and lack physical constraints such as correct interscale energy transfer and Galilean invariance.
A.motivation: Stable, accurate, and interpretable subgrid-scale closures are essential for reliable LES, and coupling large language model hypothesis generation with physics-constrained symbolic regression offers a path to automated discovery that current data-driven methods do not provide.
A.proposed_approach: The proposed framework is an autonomous research agent that iteratively generates candidate expression libraries using LLM hypothesis generation, evaluates them via a priori statistical metrics and a posteriori LES stability checks, and refines functional forms through feedback loops that incorporate physical constraints such as interscale energy transfer bounds. The abstract outlines experimental application to two-dimensional turbulent flows and convective systems, with benchmarking against standard eddy-viscosity models and unconstrained sparse regression techniques.
A.research_plan: The evidence is an experimental validation outline: apply the framework to two-dimensional turbulent flows and convective systems, use a priori statistical metrics and a posteriori LES stability checks to evaluate candidate closures, and benchmark discovered closures against standard eddy-viscosity models and unconstrained sparse regression techniques. The abstract does not state explicit quantitative failure conditions or matched compute budgets.

B.problem: Subgrid-scale closure models for large-eddy simulation of complex turbulent flows rely heavily on traditional algebraic and dynamic models that struggle with numerical stability, backscatter representation, and generalization across varying regimes. Recent LLM-based discovery methods lack active multi-scale experimental probing and fail to systematically enforce physical principles during interactive discovery loops.
B.motivation: Better subgrid-scale closures would improve large-eddy simulation reliability for complex turbulent flows, and recent LLM capabilities make autonomous, constrained discovery loops tractable.
B.proposed_approach: An autonomous multi-agent framework treats subgrid-scale closure discovery as a principled uncertainty reduction task within interactive large-eddy simulation environments. It integrates specialized LLM agents for hypothesis generation, symbolic algebraic formulation, topological simulation execution via OpenFOAM/LES platforms, and principle-aware verification. Physical constraints and active probing of out-of-distribution turbulent flows are embedded into the agents' reward and iteration loops.
B.research_plan: The paper supports its claims through a comparative evaluation of discovered closure models against traditional hand-crafted and static machine-learning baselines. The abstract does not specify metrics, flow cases, ablations, or failure conditions; the interaction loop with principle-aware verification and active out-of-distribution probing is presented as evidence of constraint satisfaction but without an explicit success criterion.

A.problem: Existing research-idea generation systems either measure novelty of finished papers after the fact or guide generation with learned or self-evaluation judges; no retrieved system uses a live topic-model density landscape of the literature as an explicit control signal during the generation loop.
A.motivation: Bibliometric findings indicate that novelty can be double-edged and has an inverted-U relationship with downstream outcomes, so steering generation toward a moderate novelty band may improve the joint novelty–feasibility of generated ideas.
A.proposed_approach: A closed-loop ideation controller maps the current literature into a continuous density landscape of idea-space using a topic model in the style of BERTopic. Each candidate research idea is positioned in that landscape via its topic-combination profile. A steering module biases each generation round toward a targeted novelty band—moderate sparsity rather than maximal—using an interpretable relative-density reward plus a grounding-based feasibility anchor.
A.research_plan: (1) The first claim is tested by comparing the density-steered controller against judge-only search (Nova) and retrieve-iterate-compare (SciMON) baselines on expert-rated novelty, with feasibility as a non-inferiority constraint. (2) The second claim is tested by comparing moderate and maximal novelty setpoints on a joint novelty–feasibility objective. The pre-registered failure condition is that if the density reward adds nothing beyond black-box judge scores, the controller collapses to a re-ranker and the core claim is falsified, demoting the work to a post-hoc analysis.

B.problem: Autonomous AI-scientist systems generate hypotheses from whatever text the agent happens to retrieve, and their success criteria carry no principled notion of which part of the literature has already been explored.
B.motivation: A principled topic map of explored literature makes novelty and integrity measurable in-pipeline, enabling deliberate exploration of underexplored but literature-supported areas and detection of selection bias and metric-misuse failures.
B.proposed_approach: The proposed framework uses one fixed, unsupervised topic map of a field corpus built from a frozen paragraph-embedding-to-topic-simplex projection trained once per corpus. This map supplies a corpus geometry that quantifies hypothesis novelty as divergence from the aggregate topic distribution of explored literature, weighted by per-cell under-coverage. It also provides a steering objective for an exploration-constrained LLM agent loop that directs the experiment-manager agent toward underexplored but literature-supported topic cells. A final audit head consumes both paper text and execution trace to flag topic-space inconsistencies such as conclusions disconnected from cited sources, claims about never-explored regions, and results clustered in an atypically narrow topic-space region.
B.research_plan: Evaluation covers a synthetic corpus with planted sparse topic cells, the BioVerge biomedical benchmark, and a controlled failure-mode corpus with injected violations patterned after documented AI-scientist failures. Under three pre-registered falsifiable claims, the framework is compared to LLM-judge and no-guidance baselines for novelty at matched claim-accuracy; the coverage footprint of generated hypothesis sets is measured to test the steering claim; and audit detection of injected integrity violations is compared with paper-only heuristics by AUC. Support for each claim requires the corresponding comparative difference to be observed; the design holds claim-accuracy matched for the novelty comparison. No additional ablations or robustness checks are described.

A.problem: Current AI systems for scientific discovery generate hypotheses and conduct experiments, but few systematically use topic modeling as an autonomous exploratory tool.
A.motivation: Autonomous topic modeling could let scientific discovery systems analyze latent document structure and detect emerging research directions without relying on static pipelines or manual human-guided analysis.
A.proposed_approach: An LLM-based autonomous agent that searches the hyperparameter space of neural topic models (embedding architecture, cluster count, clustering parameters), evaluates candidate configurations with interpretability and coherence metrics, generates natural language topic descriptions with reasoning, and detects emerging research directions through topic evolution over time. A benchmark suite is constructed from scientific corpora to evaluate autonomous topic discovery agents.
A.research_plan: (1) The performance claim is evaluated on the benchmark suite by comparing discovered topics against static topic modeling pipelines and manual human-guided approaches using coherence, interpretability, novelty, and computational cost; the claim would fail if the agent did not produce more coherent, interpretable, and novel topics at lower computational cost. (2) The bridge claim is supported by demonstrating autonomous hyperparameter optimization and analysis of latent document structure on scientific corpora.

B.problem: Autonomous research systems have not been applied to classical and interpretable statistical methods such as topic modeling, leaving practitioners to manually navigate diverse model families and tune numerous hyperparameters.
B.motivation: Automating topic model discovery and configuration would substantially reduce expert effort and make systematic comparison of model families and hyperparameters tractable across document corpora.
B.proposed_approach: The proposed autonomous agent system discovers, configures, and evaluates topic models across document corpora with minimal human input. It combines LLM-driven architecture search across topic model families, agent-guided Bayesian hyperparameter optimization, multi-criteria evaluation integrating quantitative metrics with LLM-based qualitative assessment, and automated scientific reporting.
B.research_plan: The evaluation runs the system on benchmark document collections and compares its discovered configurations and generated comparative findings against hand-tuned baselines. Support requires near-optimal configurations as judged by quantitative and LLM-based qualitative evaluation and findings that match or exceed the baselines; failure would be configurations or reports not meeting that standard under the claimed reduction in expert effort.
